under.name: Game rules
under.description: The Game rules section contains the TIME S:YSTEM rules, including phase structure, major and minor actions, combat time, and travel.

under.name: ⏳ TIME S:YSTEM
under.description: The ⏳ TIME S:YSTEM section presents rules for phase structure, major actions, minor actions, combat time, travel, phase carryover, and phase tracking.

under.name: 1. Phase Structure
under.description: The 1. Phase Structure section states that a full day is divided into nine phases, each a fixed unit of meaningful activity time.

under.name: 2. Outside Phase Rule (Major Actions)
under.description: The 2. Outside Phase Rule (Major Actions) section defines major activities as consuming phase time and gives examples, with one major activity consuming one phase unless modified.

under.name: 3. Within Phase Rule (Minor Actions)
under.description: The 3. Within Phase Rule (Minor Actions) section describes minor actions as occurring inside a phase without consuming additional time and allows unlimited such actions unless they escalate into major tasks.

under.name: 4. Combat Time Rule
under.description: The 4. Combat Time Rule section states that combat is time-compressed, with one combat encounter costing 0.5 phase, and notes cumulative tracking and rounding after the scene ends.

under.name: 5. Travel Rule
under.description: The 5. Travel Rule section states that travel cost depends on distance and difficulty, with short distance having no cost, moderate distance costing 0.5 phase, and long distance costing 1 phase or more.

under.name: 6. Phase Carryover Rule
under.description: The 6. Phase Carryover Rule section groups logically continuous related actions into a single phase, such as hunt, kill, harvest, and move within a zone.

under.name: 7. Phase Tracking Rule
under.description: The 7. Phase Tracking Rule section instructs stating the current phase, phases consumed, and next phase after every major scene.

under.name: ⚙️ SYSTEM INTENT
under.description: The ⚙️ SYSTEM INTENT section states that the structure keeps time trackable and enforceable, gives actions clear cost, lets the world react dynamically, and applies disruption pressure to routine.

under.name: 🌍 Dynamic World Event Engine
under.description: The 🌍 Dynamic World Event Engine section covers the engine's core purpose, event triggers, the number pool, and changing the pool.

under.name: 1. Core Purpose
under.description: The 1. Core Purpose section states that the Dynamic World Event Engine adds variety, opportunities, complications, and unexpected developments using a changing number pool that must reflect current world state.

under.name: 2. Event Triggers
under.description: The 2. Event Triggers section defines an event trigger as an event category and lists default triggers such as Monsters, Business, People, Weather, and Nothing.

under.name: 3. The Number Pool
under.description: The 3. The Number Pool section states that the engine uses numbers 1–100, with each trigger owning an explicit list where each number represents a 1% chance.

under.name: Pool Rules
under.description: The Pool Rules section specifies that each number belongs to exactly one trigger, all pools together contain every number from 1–100, numbers need not be consecutive, and an empty pool has a 0% chance.

under.name: Example Starting Pool
under.description: The Example Starting Pool section provides an example table assigning number pools and chances to Monsters, Business, People, Weather, and Nothing.

under.name: 4. Changing the Pool
under.description: The 4. Changing the Pool section explains that pool changes occur when actions or developments meaningfully affect an event category's likelihood and gives examples of developments and possible pool changes.

under.name: 5. Number Transfer Rule
under.description: The Number Transfer Rule requires the combined pool to contain exactly 100 numbers, with gains matched by losses.

under.name: Example: Advertising a Shop
under.description: The Example: Advertising a Shop shows Business gaining five numbers from Nothing, with before-and-after pools and Business increasing from 20% to 25% while Nothing decreases from 25% to 20%.

under.name: 6. Adjustment Size and Duration
under.description: Section 6 lists factors affecting pool adjustment size and states temporary adjustments must record expiry conditions and be reversed when they end.

under.name: 7. Event Check Timing
under.description: Section 7 specifies one event check at the start of each game day, with additional checks after entering a substantially different location, completing a major operation, or reaching another meaningful story transition.

under.name: 8. Event Roll Procedure
under.description: Section 8 lists the event-check procedure: review state, apply pool changes, confirm numbers 1-100 have exactly one owner, roll 1d100 once, identify the owning trigger, handle Nothing or resolve the event, and record changes.

under.name: 9. Event Tier Rule
under.description: Section 9 requires every generated event to be the player's current tier or exactly one tier higher, with a table of allowed event tiers by player tier.

under.name: 10. Generating the Specific Event
under.description: Section 10 states the selected trigger determines the category while current circumstances determine what happens within that category.

under.name: 11. Nothing Result
under.description: Section 11 states that if the roll selects Nothing, no new event is introduced by that check and existing conditions continue.

under.name: 12. Events Outside the Pool
under.description: Section 12 states the pool governs uncertain new developments and established consequences occur when their conditions are met without another event roll.

under.name: 13. Tracking and Transparency
under.description: Section 13 requires displaying the current pool and recording check timing, pool adjustments, duration, roll, selected trigger, player tier, event tier, and generated event.

under.name: Core Principle
under.description: The Core Principle states that actions change the odds, the roll selects the event category, and world conditions shape the event within the allowed tier range.

under.name: 1. Rest Recovery by Duration
under.description: Section 1 provides rest recovery by uninterrupted rest duration, restoring 25%, 50%, or 100% of maximum HP, MP, and SP for 0.5, 1, or 2 phase rests.

under.name: 2. Passive Non-Combat Recovery
under.description: Section 2 states that while outside active combat resolution, characters naturally recover resources over time.

under.name: Passive Recovery Rate
under.description: Passive Recovery Rate restores 10% of maximum HP, MP, and SP when the character is not in active combat, not under a recovery-blocking effect, and the environment reasonably allows natural recovery.

under.name: 3. Daily Minimum Rest Requirement
under.description: Section 3 requires all player characters to obtain at least 2 total phases of rest per day, with listed possible consequences for failure unless explicitly overridden.

under.name: 4. Recovery Basis Rule
under.description: Section 4 states that unless explicitly stated otherwise, all percentage-based recovery is calculated from maximum HP, MP, and SP rather than current values.

under.name: 5. Recovery Stacking Rule
under.description: Section 5 states that multiple valid recovery effects stack additively and combine unless a rule explicitly prevents stacking.

under.name: 6. Full Rest Rule
under.description: Section 6 classifies a completed 2-Phase Rest as a Full Rest, which restores 100% HP, MP, and SP unless modified and also satisfies the standard daily rest requirement.

under.name: 7. Rest Tracking Rule
under.description: Section 7 requires recording rest duration, recovery percentages, exact HP, MP, and SP restored, active recovery modifiers, and whether the daily minimum rest requirement has been fulfilled.

under.name: ⚔️ COMBAT SYSTEM
under.description: The Combat System section covers combat types, core combat model, initiative system, and action economy.

under.name: 1. Combat Types
under.description: Section defining the two combat types, Narrative Combat and Rules Combat, with their triggers and uses.

under.name: Narrative Combat
under.description: Subsection describing Narrative Combat, triggered when Difficulty Ratio > 0.5, resolved narratively with resource tracking.

under.name: Rules Combat
under.description: Subsection describing Rules Combat, triggered when the outcome is uncertain or contested, used for comparable enemies, dangerous encounters, tactical fights, and boss battles.

under.name: 2. Core Combat Model
under.description: Section introducing the core combat model, including the Action–Reaction System and Exchange System.

under.name: Action–Reaction System
under.description: Subsection explaining that combat resolves through Action versus Reaction rather than attack versus defense, with examples.

under.name: Exchange System
under.description: Subsection describing the Exchange System's five-step sequence and noting that multiple exchanges form a single encounter.

under.name: 3. Initiative System
under.description: Section defining Initiative as AGI + INT and stating rules for acting first and tie resolution.

under.name: 4. Action Economy
under.description: Section describing action economy, covering Major Actions limited to one per battle exchange and Minor Actions unlimited within reason.

under.name: Major Action (Limit: 1 per battle exchange)
under.description: Subsection listing examples of Major Actions, limiting them to one per battle exchange, with a boss exception.

under.name: Minor Actions (Unlimited, within reason)
under.description: Subsection listing examples of Minor Actions as unlimited within reason and noting they cannot replace a major action.

under.name: 5. Core Resolution Formula
under.description: Section covering the core resolution formula, including Action/Reaction Value, multi-stat actions, combat approach, reaction reference, outcome resolution, and effects.

under.name: Action / Reaction Value
under.description: Subsection giving the Total Power formula as Relevant Stat + Modifiers + Skill/Spell + Curved d20 + combat approach.

under.name: Multi-Stat Actions
under.description: Subsection explaining that multiple applicable stats are averaged for the Relevant Stat, with examples.

under.name: combat Approach
under.description: Subsection describing combat approach as planning, method, ingenuity, and tactics, with tier scaling.

under.name: Reaction Reference (NPC Baseline)
under.description: Subsection listing NPC baseline Reaction Reference ranges by tier and noting variation by domain.

under.name: Outcome Resolution
under.description: Subsection defining Outcome as Action Total minus Reaction Total, with positive/negative results and margin strength.

under.name: Effects
under.description: Subsection listing effects as Damage = Outcome and Buff/Debuff = Outcome ÷ 5.

under.name: 6. Combat Loop
under.description: Section outlining the five-step combat loop: declare action, declare reaction, calculate totals, compute outcome, and apply effects.

under.name: 7. Modifier Rule (Absolute)
under.description: Section stating Total Modifier is the sum of all relevant bonuses with no weighting, diminishing returns, or hidden scaling.

under.name: 7A. Combat Modifier-Sweep Transparency
under.description: Section requiring combat modifier transparency by listing included and excluded relevant modifiers and prohibiting hidden bonuses, generic tier shortcuts, or unexplained omissions.

under.name: 8. Action Validity System (Critical)
under.description: Presents the Action Validity System, including validity and numerical resolution layers, domain examples, and the core law that capability determines if an action works while numbers determine how well.

under.name: Layer 1 — Validity Check
under.description: States that the first validity-check layer asks whether the action can logically solve the problem and that a NO result means the action fails immediately.

under.name: Layer 2 — Numerical Resolution
under.description: States that if the Layer 1 validity check is YES, the formula is applied for numerical resolution.

under.name: Domain Examples
under.description: Lists invalid, valid, and partial domain examples comparing prediction actions against explosion, linear attack, and multi-hit attack scenarios.

under.name: Core Law
under.description: States the core law that capability determines whether an action works and numbers determine how well it works.

under.name: 9. Combo Action
under.description: Describes Combo Action as sequential combined actions whose value is a Relationship-Tier Combo with no member cap and no longer using the former Team Action Value formula.

under.name: Team Action Value Formula
under.description: Defines the Team Action Value Formula in which the Main is the final attacker and each sub contributes a boost based on relationship tier multiplied by the sub's own Action value, with accumulated boosts and no averaging.

under.name: Boost Table
under.description: Provides a boost table mapping relationship tiers from −5 to +5 to tier names and contribution percentages, with none for negative tiers and +1% through +50% for nonnegative tiers.

under.name: Premises that must be met
under.description: Lists pre-conditions requiring the same target and same intent before a combo begins, plus a per-stage contact gate requiring each stage's Action value including accumulated bonus to exceed the opponent's Action value.

under.name: Worked Example
under.description: Shows a worked example of four attackers at Action value 30 and Deep Bond (+10%) with Main, yielding cumulative values 30, 33, 36, and 39.

under.name: Failure Rule
under.description: Describes pre-condition failure making a combo invalid and contact-gate failure collapsing a valid combo, with notes on member cap, per-member minimum, and node relationship tier records.

under.name: 10. Combat Rules Extensions
under.description: Presents combat rules extensions covering multi-target attacks, counters, reinforcements, action interruption, traps, environmental manipulation, and death rules.

under.name: Multi-Target Attacks
under.description: States that multi-target attacks use one action with separate resolution per target.

under.name: Counter Mechanic
under.description: States that a counter counts as a reaction and cannot be used if the reaction is already spent.

under.name: Reinforcement Rule
under.description: States that new enemies create a new encounter, resetting major actions and reactions and recalculating initiative.

under.name: Action Interruption
under.description: States that if a character is eliminated before acting, the action is lost.

under.name: Trap System
under.description: States that trap creation occurs outside combat and trap activation is a minor action.

under.name: Environmental Manipulation
under.description: States that environmental manipulation can force reactions, apply penalties, and alter the battlefield.

under.name: Death Rule
under.description: States that HP = 0 results in death and that there are no default unconscious states or death saves.

under.name: 11. Resource Tracking
under.description: States that HP, MP, and SP should always be tracked, even in narrative combat.

under.name: 12. Encounter Timing
under.description: Describes encounter timing rules, stating that 1 encounter equals 0.5 phase and 2 encounters equal 1 phase.

under.name: Harvest Rule
under.description: Covers immediate post-combat harvesting and states that it adds no extra phase unless complex.

under.name: 13. Boss Rules
under.description: Lists possible boss features as multiple major actions, multiple reactions, additional phases, and unique mechanics.

under.name: 🧪 NON-COMBAT SYSTEM
under.description: Covers the non-combat system, including action sources, the action system, the Resolution Assembly Protocol, institutional standing, practice carryover, and facility modifier bands.

under.name: 1. Action Sources
under.description: Lists non-combat action sources as Crafting, Research, Engineering, Exploration, Training, and Economy.

under.name: 2. Action System
under.description: Describes the non-combat action system, including the action value formula and Realistic Approach execution-quality scaling.

under.name: Action value
under.description: Gives the action value formula as average relevant stats plus modifiers plus d20 plus Realistic Approach.

under.name: Realistic Approach (Execution Quality)
under.description: Defines Realistic Approach (Execution Quality) as planning, method, tools, and preparation, with tier-based scaling from 5–10 at Tier 0 to 500+ at Tier 6.

under.name: 2A. Resolution Assembly Protocol (Mandatory)
under.description: Mandates assembling every meaningful noncombat action from its specific domain before resolution through domain definition, stat selection, modifier sweeps, task-building, scaling, and transparent resolution.

under.name: 1. Define the Domain and Method
under.description: Instructs stating what is actually being attempted and how, with examples such as batch craft, sale contract, field preservation, mana training, research experiment, or political negotiation.

under.name: 2. Select Relevant Stats
under.description: Instructs using only the stat or multi-stat average that the method genuinely demands.

under.name: 3. Perform a Modifier Sweep
under.description: Instructs checking all possible modifier sources and listing included and excluded modifiers with reasons.

under.name: 4. Build Task from World Reality
under.description: States that task values are independent of the actor’s ECS and must reflect actual requirements such as market demand, institutional power, recipe complexity, batch scale, tool quality, material risk, social leverage, and environmental conditions.

under.name: 5. Apply Real-World Scaling
under.description: Describes interpreting the completed Action or Task value through Value ÷ 5 human-equivalent capability without altering the mechanical value.

under.name: 6. Resolve Transparently
under.description: States Outcome = Action Value − Task Value and prohibits hidden bonuses, generic tier shortcuts, or automatic success after calculation.

under.name: ECS Boundary
under.description: Defines ECS as the total of core stats used where an ECS rule explicitly calls for it and not as a replacement for a domain-specific Action or Task value.

under.name: 2B. Institutional Standing from Noncash Gains
under.description: Describes Institutional Standing from documented noncash gains, tracked as 0–10 scores that grant fitting domain modifiers and are not automatic social control.

under.name: 2C. Outcome-Based Practice Carryover and Derived Refinement
under.description: Describes outcome-based Practice Carryover for repeated logged practice with the same narrow method, including cumulative P adjustments and chain-breaking conditions.

under.name: Derived Refinement, Branching, and Combined Lineage
under.description: Describes refining a documented technique into a new related technique when predecessors have recorded uncapped raw outcomes of +10 or higher, including lineage modifier calculation and double-counting limits.

under.name: 2D. Facility Modifier Bands
under.description: Describes location-bound facility modifiers for functioning facilities, with Tier 1 facility modifiers from +2 to +5 and a requirement to list active facilities in the Ledger’s Facility Modifier Index.

under.name: 2E. Distinct Cognitive-Assistance Modifiers
under.description: Section 2E defines distinct cognitive-assistance modifiers for a Knowledge Database Rune and Ava/Analyst Mirror, including additive bonuses, combined synergy, and scope limits.

under.name: 2F. Routine Validated Production
under.description: Section 2F defines routine validated production as repeating a proven recipe, materials, facility, template, and completed scale without a roll, with rolls required when circumstances change materially.

under.name: 3. Task System
under.description: Section 3 presents the Task System, including task value, difficulty scaling, novelty scaling, and integration, independence, and field-risk factors.

under.name: Task Value
under.description: Task Value subsection states that Task equals Difficulty plus Novelty plus applicable Integration, Independence, and Field-Risk factors, each real, stated, and non-overlapping.

under.name: Difficulty Scaling
under.description: Difficulty Scaling subsection lists difficulty ranges for Tiers 0 through 6, from 20-50 at Tier 0 to 2000+ at Tier 6.

under.name: Novelty Scaling
under.description: Novelty Scaling subsection lists novelty ranges for Tiers 0 through 6, from 10-20 at Tier 0 to 1000+ at Tier 6.

under.name: Integration / Independence / Field-Risk Factors
under.description: Integration / Independence / Field-Risk Factors subsection gives point ranges for integration, independence, and field risk and instructs using only factors actually present and not double-counting.

under.name: 3A. Permanent Advancement Task Floors
under.description: Section 3A sets starting Task floors for permanent advancement attempts, including new independent and derived Tier 1 modifiers, multi-domain techniques, and Tier 2 breakthroughs.

under.name: 4. Outcome Resolution
under.description: Section 4 defines Outcome Resolution as Action value minus Task with a cap of +10 and includes outcome results and failure consequences.

under.name: Outcome Results
under.description: Outcome Results subsection maps outcome ranges from less than -5 to 5 to Great Failure through Great Success.

under.name: Failure Consequences
under.description: Failure Consequences subsection describes Great Failure as destruction, injury, or death; Failure as loss of materials; and Partial Failure as flawed output plus learning.

under.name: 5. Action Time
under.description: Action Time section categorizes basic, Simple, Advanced, and Major actions as within Phase, 1 Phase, multiple Phases, and Days respectively.

under.name: 6. Collaborative Action
under.description: Section 6 covers Collaborative Action, including the Team Action value formula and behavior of team contributions.

under.name: Team Action value Formula
under.description: Team Action value Formula subsection defines the lead as Main, subs as other participants, and Team Action value as Main's Action value plus the sum of each sub's relationship-tier boost times that sub's Action value.

under.name: Behavior
under.description: Behavior subsection describes collaborative action behavior: strongest member defines baseline, team adds proportional amplification, weak members contribute less, and strong members scale output significantly.

under.name: ⚙️ SYSTEM SUMMARY
under.description: SYSTEM SUMMARY subsection states the system ensures no ambiguity through numerical resolution, no hidden scaling, skill expression via action validity, and balance through domain constraints.

under.name: Consumable Growth and Reward System
under.description: Consumable Growth and Reward System section covers XP, temporary modifiers, and effect modifiers from food, pills, potions, herbs, and edible harvest substances, plus reward determinants and core rules.

under.name: Overview
under.description: Overview subsection states that food, pills, potions, herbs, and edible harvest substances can grant XP, temporary modifiers, and effect modifiers, with rewards determined by consumable tier, material quality, production difficulty, creator skill, and character tier.

under.name: Core Rules
under.description: Core Rules subsection covers tier restrictions, material consistency, effect modifier restrictions including the same-material rule, and permanent effect modifier requirements.

under.name: Tier Restrictions
under.description: Tier Restrictions subsection states a character cannot gain any effect from consumables below their own tier, while XP rewards and temporary modifiers are repeatable and may come from consumables above their tier, with an example about a Tier 0 character consuming Tier 4 food.

under.name: Example
under.description: The example states that a Tier 0 character consuming Tier 4 food may still gain the XP reward and temporary modifier but may not safely integrate permanent effects beyond their capability.

under.name: Material Consistency
under.description: Material consistency requires that materials used for food, pills, and potions match the tier of the final product, so higher-tier products cannot be created from lower-tier materials alone.

under.name: Effect Modifier Restrictions
under.description: Effect Modifier Restrictions states that effect modifiers are tightly controlled and contains a Same-Material Rule subsection.

under.name: Same-Material Rule
under.description: The Same-Material Rule allows a character to gain a permanent effect modifier only once from the same meal, herb, edible harvest substance, potion, or products created from the same core materials, preventing permanent stat farming.

under.name: Permanent Effect Modifier Requirements
under.description: Permanent effect modifiers require minimum Tier 3 item quality, meaningful biological or magical integration, and sufficient potency, with additional requirements for food and alchemical effects.

under.name: Food
under.description: Permanent food effects require a chef of equal or higher tier than the consumable.

under.name: pills and potions
under.description: Permanent alchemical effects require an alchemist of equal or higher tier than the consumable.

under.name: Food Rewards
under.description: The Food Rewards table lists XP and temporary modifier rewards by tier from Base through Tier 6, with upper tiers also listing effect modifiers.

under.name: Pills and Potions Rewards
under.description: The Pills and Potions Rewards table lists XP and temporary modifier rewards by tier from Tier 0 through Tier 6, with upper tiers also listing effect modifiers.

under.name: Herb and Edible Harvest Rewards
under.description: The Herb and Edible Harvest Rewards table lists XP and temporary modifier rewards by tier from Tier 0 through Tier 6, with upper tiers also listing effect modifiers.

under.name: Specialized Consumables
under.description: Specialized consumables are herbs, foods, and alchemical products that provide direct functional effects such as healing, detoxification, hallucinations, poison, regeneration, stamina or mana restoration, sensory enhancement, sleep induction, or emotional suppression instead of XP.

under.name: Example
under.description: The example states that a Tier 0 healing potion restores 10-50 HP rather than granting XP.

under.name: Design Logic
under.description: Design Logic explains that higher-tier consumables are difficult to acquire, higher-tier food and alchemical products require skilled preparation or specialized knowledge, raw herbs are easier to obtain, and permanent modifiers should feel meaningful, rare, and earned.

under.name: Balance Notes
under.description: Balance Notes contains a Food subsection stating that food may grant greater rewards than raw herbs because it combines multiple ingredients, preparation techniques, and creator skill.

under.name: Food
under.description: The Food subsection of Balance Notes states that food may grant greater rewards than raw herbs because it combines multiple ingredients, preparation techniques, and creator skill.

under.name: pills and potions
under.description: The pills and potions balance subsection states that pills and potions grant the highest rewards because they are highly refined, specialized, resource intensive, and heavily tier-gated.

under.name: Permanent Effects
under.description: Permanent effect modifiers begin at Tier 3, are intentionally rare, and are not meant to be farmed repeatedly.

under.name: Repeatability Rules
under.description: Repeatability Rules includes a Repeatable subsection stating that XP and temporary modifiers may be repeatedly gained with no hard repeat limit unless specifically stated by an item.

under.name: Repeatable
under.description: The Repeatable subsection states that XP and temporary modifiers may be repeatedly gained, with no hard repeat limit unless specifically stated by an item.

under.name: Crafting Output Rules
under.description: Crafting Output Rules lists potion outputs of 3 on Great Success, 2 on Success, and 1 on Partial Success; pill outputs of 5, 3, and 1 respectively; and a note that pills produce higher quantity because they are weaker and less effective per unit.

under.name: Potions
under.description: The Potions subsection under Crafting Output Rules lists potion outputs for Great Success (3), Success (2), and Partial Success (1).

under.name: Pills
under.description: The Pills subsection under Crafting Output Rules lists pill outputs for Great Success (5), Success (3), and Partial Success (1).

under.name: Note
under.description: The Note subsection states that pills produce a higher quantity than potions because they are weaker and less effective per unit.

under.name: Restricted
under.description: The Restricted subsection lists the same-material rule, creator tier requirements, minimum item tier requirements, and meaningful integration conditions as restrictions on permanent effect modifiers, which are not freely repeatable.

under.name: STAT SYSTEM
under.description: The STAT SYSTEM section contains the CORE STAT SYSTEM heading and begins defining individual stats such as Strength, Agility, Endurance, Intelligence, and Wisdom.

under.name: 🧬 CORE STAT SYSTEM
under.description: The CORE STAT SYSTEM subsection defines core stats including Strength, Agility, Endurance, Intelligence, and Wisdom with their governed actions, effects, and penalties.

under.name: 1. STRENGTH (STR)
under.description: The STRENGTH (STR) subsection defines raw physical force and lists what it governs, its effects, and penalties when STR is below 3.

under.name: 2. AGILITY (AGI)
under.description: The AGILITY (AGI) subsection defines speed, reflex, coordination, and precision and lists what it governs, its effects, and penalties when AGI is below 3.

under.name: 3. ENDURANCE (END)
under.description: The ENDURANCE (END) subsection defines physical resilience and sustained capability and lists what it governs, its effects, and penalties when END is below 3.

under.name: 4. INTELLIGENCE (INT)
under.description: The INTELLIGENCE (INT) subsection defines logic, analysis, and structured thinking and lists what it governs, its effects, and penalties when INT is below 3.

under.name: 5. WISDOM (WIS)
under.description: The WISDOM (WIS) subsection defines mana control, intuition, and awareness and lists what it governs, its effects, and penalties when WIS is below 3.

under.name: 6. PRESENCE (PRE)
under.description: The PRESENCE (PRE) subsection defines influence exerted through aura and identity and lists what it governs, its effects, and penalties when PRE is below 3.

under.name: ⚙️ DERIVED STATS
under.description: The DERIVED STATS subsection presents formulas calculated from core stats for HP, MP, Stamina, Initiative, and Carry Load.

under.name: Resistances
under.description: The Resistances subsection lists Physical resistance as END, Magical as INT + WIS, Mental as WIS, and Social as PRE.

under.name: 🧩 MODIFIER SYSTEM
under.description: The MODIFIER SYSTEM section defines modifiers as performance beyond base stats and begins with the Core Principle and Stat Modifiers subsections.

under.name: Core Principle
under.description: The Core Principle subsection states that modifiers define performance beyond base stats and lists stats, class, effects, equipment, and situation as sources.

under.name: 1. Stat Modifiers
under.description: The 1. Stat Modifiers subsection describes broad stat-bound capabilities, creation fields, examples, rules, and combination examples.

under.name: 2. Modifier Count Scaling
under.description: The Modifier Count Scaling subsection maps stat values 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, and 1000 to modifier counts from 1 to 8.

under.name: 3. Stat Modifier and Class Modifier Tier Review
under.description: The Stat Modifier and Class Modifier Tier Review subsection requires reviewing all Stat and Class Modifiers when a character advances to a new Tier and lists evidence considerations for magnitude changes.

under.name: Examples
under.description: The Examples subsection shows an END SKILL example called Hard bone that boosts defence and body strength by +20.

under.name: Class Modifiers
under.description: Class Modifiers are class-specific capabilities granted through an acquired class and its progression, with creation fields, examples, and tier-related notes.

under.name: Tier Review
under.description: Class Modifiers are reviewed when a character advances to a new Tier, and magnitude may increase only with stronger evidence and within the applicable Tier strength band.

under.name: Examples
under.description: The Examples subsection lists a Swift Blade class modifier example that boosts blade attacks, blade speed, and blade movements by +4.

under.name: Effect Modifier
under.description: Effect Modifiers are narrow, reusable techniques or action patterns with activation conditions, limitations, growth boundaries, stacking rules, and action-history justification.

under.name: 1. Sources of New Effect Modifiers
under.description: This subsection lists sources for gaining a new effect modifier, including repeated successful use, experimentation, training breakthroughs, combat adaptation, specialization, proven behavior under pressure, and consumption.

under.name: 2. Threshold
under.description: This subsection states that a new effect modifier may be gained only through repeated meaningful success, a major breakthrough event, or successful creation through the experimentation system.

under.name: 3. Strength
under.description: This subsection requires new effect modifiers to obey existing tier strength ranges, with examples of +1 to +2 at Tier 0 and +2 to +5 at Tier 1.

under.name: 4. Development from Zero
under.description: This subsection states that, except during first-day character creation, every new Effect Modifier begins at magnitude 0 and must be groomed through meaningful effort and evidence-based review.

under.name: 5. Anti-Abuse Rules
under.description: This subsection states that effect modifiers cannot be farmed freely and introduces hard limits, including restrictions on duplicates, trivial farming, broadness, and justification.

under.name: Hard limits
under.description: The Hard limits subsection lists prohibitions on duplicate effect modifiers from the same behavior, trivial farming, unjustified or overly broad modifiers, and vague concepts such as "good fighter" or "smart planner".

under.name: 6. Upgrade Rule
under.description: This subsection states that effect modifiers do not automatically grow with level or tier and must be actively integrated and refined through use, experimentation, training, or breakthrough.

under.name: 7. Modifier Identity Rule
under.description: This subsection requires every new effect modifier to have a name, tier, short description, and clear boost domain, with a Wolf Pattern example.

under.name: Equipment Modifiers
under.description: Equipment Modifiers come from a specific owned, available, or equipped item and apply only while the item is present and within scope, with creation fields and examples.

under.name: Examples
under.description: The Examples subsection lists an Assassin cloak equipment modifier that boosts hidden, ambush attack, and stealth by +2.

under.name: Situational Modifiers
under.description: Situational Modifiers come from temporary circumstances, apply only while the stated context exists, and are not automatically stored as other modifier types.

under.name: Modifier Behavior Rules
under.description: The Modifier Behavior Rules section lists principles such as only relevant modifiers applying, some modifiers unlocking mechanics, alignment increasing effectiveness, and modifiers defining build identity.

under.name: Modifier Strength by Tier
under.description: The Modifier Strength by Tier subsection states that non-situational modifiers scale by Tier from +1 to +2 at Tier 0 through +50 to +100 at Tier 5.

under.name: ⚠️ SCALING REALITY
under.description: The Scaling Reality section notes that at higher tiers modifier stacking grows exponentially and that control comes from action validity, domain limits, and counterplay.

under.name: 🔥 ACTIVE SKILL SYSTEM
under.description: The Active Skill System section covers tier determination, skill tiers, and skill creation, with tier effects and costs.

under.name: 1. Tier Determination
under.description: The Tier Determination subsection defines a skill’s tier by the highest of power output, area of effect, conceptual complexity, and energy cost.

under.name: 2. Skill Tiers
under.description: Skill Tiers section lists Tier 0 through Tier 6 with their effect ranges and MP/SP costs.

under.name: Tier 0 — Human Level
under.description: Tier 0 — Human Level describes small, single-target, low-cost skills with an effect of +10 to +15 and costs of 2–10 MP and 2–10 SP.

under.name: Tier 1 — Superhuman
under.description: Tier 1 — Superhuman describes enhanced-force, moderate-impact skills with an effect of +20 to +45 and costs of 10–20 MP and 10–20 SP.

under.name: Tier 2 — Village Level
under.description: Tier 2 — Village Level describes wide-AoE, high-impact skills with an effect of +50 to +95 and costs of 20–50 MP and 20–50 SP.

under.name: Tier 3 — City Level
under.description: Tier 3 — City Level describes massive-scale, war-impacting skills with an effect of +100 to +190 and costs of 50–100 MP and 50–100 SP.

under.name: Tier 4 — National Level
under.description: Tier 4 — National Level describes skills that alter regions with an effect of +200 to +480 and costs of 100–200 MP and 100–200 SP.

under.name: Tier 5 — Continental Level
under.description: Tier 5 — Continental Level describes skills that reshape landmass with an effect of +500 to +990 and costs of 200–500 MP and 200–500 SP.

under.name: Tier 6 — World Level
under.description: Tier 6 — World Level describes extreme, non-mortal skills with an effect of 1000+ and costs of 500+ MP and 500+ SP.

under.name: 3. Skill Creation
under.description: Skill Creation section states that skill creation uses the Experimentation System, comparing action value against task difficulty and novelty, with success creating a skill.

under.name: 4. Skill Evolution
under.description: Skill Evolution section lists practice, experimentation, combination, and improved control as ways skills evolve, with an example path from Mana Missile to Mana Constructs to Telekinetic Weapons.

under.name: 5. Skill Categories
under.description: Skill Categories section lists Combat, Movement, Support, Crafting, Infrastructure, and Economic as categories used for Action value relevance and interaction logic.

under.name: ⚙️ FINAL SYSTEM INTENT
under.description: Final System Intent section explains the system works because stats define capability domains, modifiers define execution strength, skills define application, action validity prevents abuse, and scaling is powerful but not unchecked.

under.name: IV. DUAL XP SYSTEM — THE TWO PATHS OF GROWTH
under.description: Dual XP System section introduces two separate, non-interchangeable XP systems: Normal XP for life, struggle, survival, and overall evolution, and Class XP for mastery, discipline, specialization, and role refinement.

under.name: 1. NORMAL XP SYSTEM — LIFE XP
under.description: Normal XP System — Life XP section covers broad personal growth from hardship, achievement, and meaningful action, with subsections on earning, nature, level cap, and level-up rewards.

under.name: A. How Normal XP Is Earned
under.description: How Normal XP Is Earned section states Normal XP comes from actions that meaningfully advance life, survival, or development, with examples such as defeating enemies, surviving danger, completing quests, exploring, training, crafting difficult items, and solving challenges.

under.name: B. Nature of Normal XP
under.description: Nature of Normal XP section states Normal XP reflects overall character evolution rather than specialization and tracks survival, struggle, adaptation, discovery, and achievement.

under.name: C. Level Cap
under.description: Level Cap section states Normal XP has no level cap and that characters can continue leveling indefinitely, with theoretically infinite growth.

under.name: D. Normal Level-Up Rewards
under.description: Normal Level-Up Rewards section states each Normal Level grants +15 Stat Points that may be distributed freely across the six core stats.

under.name: 2. CLASS XP SYSTEM — MASTERY XP
under.description: Class XP System — Mastery XP section covers focused growth within a chosen role, with subsections on earning, nature, level cap, and class level-up rewards.

under.name: A. How Class XP Is Earned
under.description: How Class XP Is Earned section states Class XP is earned only through unique, purposeful, class-aligned actions tied to class identity, with examples such as a warrior developing a stance or a mage performing a ritual, and awards only when the action deepens class mastery.

under.name: B. Nature of Class XP
under.description: Section B describes the nature of Class XP as reflecting specialization, discipline, technical refinement, mastery of role, and advancement within class identity.

under.name: C. Level Cap
under.description: Section C states that Class XP has no level cap and that class progression can continue indefinitely, unlocking new class modifiers.

under.name: D. Class Level-Up Rewards
under.description: Section D explains that Class Level-Ups do not grant stat points but instead grant class-based advancement such as stances, forms, passive features, transformations, and class abilities.

under.name: 3. CORE DISTINCTION
under.description: Section 3 contrasts what Normal XP gives with what Class XP gives in the dual XP system.

under.name: Normal XP gives
under.description: This subsection lists what Normal XP gives: broader growth, stat increases, overall scaling, and universal evolution.

under.name: Class XP gives
under.description: This subsection lists narrower growth, class depth, technical refinement, and specialization rewards as what Class XP gives.

under.name: 4. BASE XP
under.description: This section states that each challenge or opponent has a Base XP value determined by rarity, ecological danger, combat role, and overall significance, and it includes tier-based Base NORMAL XP and Base CLASS XP tables.

under.name: Base NORMAL XP by Tier
under.description: This subsection gives Base NORMAL XP ranges for Tiers 0 through 5, from 100 to 200 at Tier 0 up to 5000 to 10000 at Tier 5.

under.name: Base CLASS XP by Tier
under.description: This subsection gives Base CLASS XP ranges for Tiers 0 through 5, from 50 to 100 at Tier 0 up to 2000 to 5000 at Tier 5.

under.name: 5. DIFFICULTY RATIO
under.description: This section explains that Difficulty Ratio determines how meaningful the challenge was and therefore how much XP should be awarded, including combat and non-combat difficulty ratio subsections.

under.name: A. Combat Difficulty Ratio
under.description: Defines the combat difficulty ratio D using total player ECS, total enemy ECS, and a denominator based on player tier.

under.name: Interpretation
under.description: Explains that D stays near 1 when enemy power is close to player power, rises above 1 when enemy power is much higher, and drops below 1 when enemy power is far lower.

under.name: B. Non-Combat Difficulty Ratio
under.description: Defines the non-combat difficulty ratio D as Task divided by Player ECS, comparing task difficulty directly against the character’s effective capability.

under.name: 6. NON-COMBAT OUTCOME BANDS
under.description: Lists non-combat outcome bands with XP multiplier modifiers ranging from Great Success at D × 2 to Great Failure at D × 0.25.

under.name: 7. XP REWARD FORMULA
under.description: Presents the standard XP Reward = Base XP × D and, for non-combat tasks using outcome bands, XP Reward = Base XP × D × Outcome Modifier.

under.name: Standard Formula
under.description: Describes the standard XP reward formula as Base XP × D, with an outcome modifier for non-combat tasks using outcome bands.

under.name: 8. MINIMUM XP RULE
under.description: States that if the difficulty multiplier D is less than 0.3, no XP is awarded, preventing farming trivial actions or weak enemies.

under.name: 9. XP REQUIRED TO LEVEL — NORMAL XP
under.description: Presents the Normal XP Required formula as 500 × Level × (Tier + 1) for the next Normal Level.

under.name: Behavior
under.description: Lists that Normal XP requirements scale with current level, scale harder at higher tiers, and keep infinite growth possible while slowing progression naturally.

under.name: 10. XP REQUIRED TO LEVEL — CLASS XP
under.description: Presents the Class XP Required formula as 100 × Level × (Tier + 2) for the next Class Level.

under.name: Behavior
under.description: The Behavior section under 10. XP REQUIRED TO LEVEL — CLASS XP states that Class XP leveling is cheaper than Normal leveling, supports more frequent mastery progression, and keeps class growth active without overshadowing stat growth.

under.name: 11. FINAL SYSTEM LOGIC
under.description: The 11. FINAL SYSTEM LOGIC section presents Normal XP and Class XP as separate paths and lists shared rules governing both.

under.name: Normal XP
under.description: The Normal XP subsection under FINAL SYSTEM LOGIC describes Normal XP as life experience, broad evolution, and survival-based growth, and lists its reward as +15 stat points per level.

under.name: Class XP
under.description: The Class XP subsection under FINAL SYSTEM LOGIC describes Class XP as role mastery, specialization, and technical refinement, and lists modifiers as its reward.

under.name: Shared Rules
under.description: The Shared Rules subsection under FINAL SYSTEM LOGIC states that both XP paths scale infinitely, use challenge relevance, reject trivial farming, and reward meaningful progression in different ways.

under.name: 12. CLEAN SYSTEM SUMMARY
under.description: Summary section listing Normal XP and Class XP characteristics alongside XP formulas and level-up formulas.

under.name: Normal XP
under.description: Normal XP subsection describing broad growth, stat advancement, and survival and achievement basis.

under.name: Class XP
under.description: Class XP subsection describing specialized growth, mastery advancement, and class identity basis.

under.name: XP Formula
under.description: XP Formula subsection presenting XP as Base XP multiplied by a Difficulty Multiplier.

under.name: Non-Combat Version
under.description: Non-Combat Version subsection presenting XP as Base XP multiplied by Difficulty Multiplier and an Outcome Modifier.

under.name: No XP Threshold
under.description: Under Normal XP, the No XP Threshold subsection states that if D < 0.3, no XP is awarded.

under.name: Level-Up Formulas
under.description: The Level-Up Formulas subsection lists Normal XP Required = 500 × (Level − 1) × (Tier + 1) and Class XP Required = 100 × (Level − 1) × (Tier + 2).

under.name: V. CANONICAL TIER SYSTEM
under.description: Section V defines the Canonical Tier System, covering tier-level structure, stat growth, nature of tiers, and tier power scale.

under.name: 1. Tier–Level Structure
under.description: The Tier–Level Structure subsection maps Tier 0 through Tier 6 to level ranges and states that levels increase stats while tiers define what those stats can actually do.

under.name: 2. Stat Growth System
under.description: The Stat Growth System subsection states that all characters and monsters follow Total Stats = a + 15 × (Level − 1), with a as the starting stat pool and properties of linear growth.

under.name: Properties
under.description: Properties of the Stat Growth System include linear growth for predictable scaling, +15 stats per level aligned with the Normal XP system, and support for clean Action value calculation.

under.name: 3. Nature of Tiers
under.description: Nature of Tiers states that tiers are qualitative thresholds rather than merely numeric, with levels steadily increasing power and tiers unlocking new categories of impact.

under.name: 4. Tier Power Scale
under.description: Tier Power Scale presents tier definitions from Tier 0 Human Level through Tier 6 World Level with associated capability descriptions.

under.name: Tier 0 — Human Level
under.description: Tier 0 — Human Level covers peak human capability, skilled fighters, hunters, and basic mages, with no true supernatural dominance.

under.name: Tier 1 — Superhuman
under.description: Tier 1 — Superhuman covers enhanced speed and strength, combat superiority, and dominance in small engagements.

under.name: Tier 2 — Village Level
under.description: The Tier 2 — Village Level section lists area destruction, battlefield control, and the beginning of environmental impact.

under.name: Tier 3 — City Level
under.description: The Tier 3 — City Level section lists large-scale devastation, war-level influence, and strategic threat.

under.name: Tier 4 — Country Level
under.description: The Tier 4 — Country Level section lists national-scale destruction, ecosystem disruption, and large-region control.

under.name: Tier 5 — Continental Level
under.description: The Tier 5 — Continental Level section lists climate and terrain manipulation, massive-scale phenomena, and world-impacting events.

under.name: Tier 6 — World Level
under.description: The Tier 6 — World Level section lists being beyond mortal systems, requiring separate mechanics, and not being bound by standard rules.

under.name: 5. Tier Breakthrough Rule (Critical)
under.description: States that levels alone do not advance tiers and that reaching a new tier requires successfully creating a skill of the next tier.

under.name: Example
under.description: Lists examples where Tier 0 to Tier 1 requires Tier 1 skill creation and Tier 1 to Tier 2 requires Tier 2 skill creation.

under.name: Implications
under.description: Lists experimentation, knowledge, creativity, execution, and risk as factors on which tier advancement depends, with progression earned through innovation rather than grinding.

under.name: 6. Breakthrough Difficulty Scaling
under.description: Describes each tier jump as exponentially harder, from Human to Superhuman being difficult through higher tiers becoming increasingly near-impossible because each tier represents a new paradigm.

under.name: 7. Gameplay Structure
under.description: Describes a dual progression system in which levels provide steady stat growth and tiers provide breakthrough-based power evolution.

under.name: 8. Tier Interaction in Combat
under.description: In the Canonical Tier System, Tier Interaction in Combat specifies that each tier difference grants +10 to Actions and +10 to Reactions.

under.name: Meaning
under.description: The Meaning subsection states that higher-tier combatants have an inherent advantage while lower-tier fighters remain viable through strategy, preparation, teamwork, and domain advantage.

under.name: 9. Tier Utilization Rule
under.description: The Tier Utilization Rule states that characters cannot fully use higher-tier tools or abilities.

under.name: Effects of mismatch
under.description: Effects of mismatch lists instability, reduced output, backlash, and incomplete activation as consequences of tier mismatch.

under.name: 10. Equipment Scaling Rule
under.description: The Equipment Scaling Rule states that lower-tier equipment degrades under higher-tier usage, with possible outcomes including reduced effectiveness, durability failure, and structural breakage.

under.name: Possible outcomes
under.description: Lists possible equipment outcomes such as reduced effectiveness, durability failure, and structural breakage, with an example of a Tier 0 weapon breaking when used by a Tier 3 character.

under.name: VI. INTERPRETATION LAYER (REAL-WORLD SCALING)
under.description: Describes the interpretation layer for real-world scaling, including its purpose, core conversion rule, interpretation process, example, key properties, and limits.

under.name: Purpose
under.description: States that the interpretation layer's purpose is to translate abstract values into intuitive meaning.

under.name: Core Conversion Rule
under.description: Defines the core conversion rule of Multiplier = Value ÷ 5 as representing human-equivalent capability.

under.name: Interpretation Process
under.description: Outlines the interpretation process of converting via Value ÷ 5, comparing action value against task, and translating to narrative meaning.

under.name: Example
under.description: Example in the real-world scaling interpretation layer showing an action value of 300 translating to 60× human and a task of 200 translating to 40× human, concluding that capability exceeds requirement.

under.name: Key Properties
under.description: Lists key properties of the real-world scaling interpretation layer: making scaling intuitive, keeping extreme values understandable, and supporting consistent narration.

under.name: Limits
under.description: Lists limits of the real-world scaling interpretation layer: no mechanical impact, no alteration of outcomes, and no enforcement of realism.

under.name: VII. CAPABILITY INTERPRETATION SCALE
under.description: Presents the Capability Interpretation Scale table mapping multiplier ranges from 1×–2× (Peak Human) up to 500×–1000× (Conceptual) to their meanings.

under.name: Rule
under.description: States the rule that this interpretation layer explains power and does not change mechanics.

under.name: VIII. TIER-6 SYSTEM (TRANSCENDENT LAYER)
under.description: Section on the Tier-6 transcendent layer covering the nature of Tier-6 beings, archetypes, methods of influence, visibility rule, narrative layer, conflict effects, and mechanical integration.

under.name: 1. Nature of Tier-6
under.description: Subsection describing Tier-6 beings as unable to physically enter the world, existing outside the system, and operating through indirect influence.

under.name: 2. Archetypes
under.description: Subsection listing Divine, Eldritch, and Profane archetypes with associated themes of order, protection, destiny, unknown chaotic curiosity, destruction, and corruption.

under.name: 3. Methods of Influence
under.description: Subsection outlining methods of influence through blessings, champions, and subtle influence.

under.name: Blessings
under.description: Subsection on blessings as direct power grants that include abilities, luck, and resilience.

under.name: Champions
under.description: The Champions section describes one mortal per entity becoming a narrative extension, with examples such as hero, destroyer, prophet, and tyrant.

under.name: Subtle Influence
under.description: The Subtle Influence section lists dreams, intuition, coincidence, emotional shifts, and survival bias as methods of influence.

under.name: 4. Visibility Rule
under.description: The Visibility Rule section states that Tier-6 entities are invisible unless they reveal themselves or the observer has special perception.

under.name: 5. Narrative Layer
under.description: The Narrative Layer section describes the world as a cosmic observation system in which different entities favor different outcomes and multiple forces influence events simultaneously.

under.name: 6. Conflict Effects
under.description: The Conflict Effects section lists unstable fate, opposing champions, corrupted blessings, and anomalous events as effects when influences overlap.

under.name: 7. Mechanical Integration
under.description: Section 7, Mechanical Integration, states that Tier-6 influence may appear as hidden modifiers, rare abilities, artifacts, narrative pressure, or world events, with the hard rule that Tier-6 beings never directly enter the world.

under.name: ⚙️ FINAL SYSTEM INTENT
under.description: The Final System Intent section explains that the system works because levels provide predictable scaling, tiers mark meaningful breakthroughs, skills are a gateway to higher power, action value is a unified measurement, and an interpretation layer provides clarity without interference.

under.name: VI. RESOURCE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
under.description: The VI. Resource Management System section establishes that all consumable or depletable resources must be explicitly tracked, with subsections covering resource types, resource ledger logging, and passive consumption.

under.name: 1. Universal Resource Rule
under.description: The 1. Universal Resource Rule requires all consumable or depletable resources to be explicitly tracked at all times across every system layer, including combat, crafting, experimentation, spellcasting, infrastructure, travel, daily living, and trade.

under.name: 2. Resource Types
under.description: The 2. Resource Types section lists tracked resources including core HP/MP/SP, economic gold/silver/bronze, material raw materials/monster parts/herbs/alchemical ingredients/trap components, survival food/water, and system infrastructure mana/relay upkeep.

under.name: Core Resources
under.description: The Core Resources section under Resource Types lists HP (Health), MP (Mana), and SP (Stamina).

under.name: Economic Resources
under.description: The Economic Resources section under Resource Types lists Gold, Silver, and Bronze.

under.name: Material Resources
under.description: The Material Resources section under Resource Types lists raw materials, monster parts, herbs, alchemical ingredients, and trap components.

under.name: Survival Resources
under.description: The Survival Resources section under Resource Types lists food and water.

under.name: System Resources
under.description: The System Resources section under Resource Types lists infrastructure mana and relay/system upkeep.

under.name: 3. Resource Ledger Rule
under.description: This rule requires every action that consumes resources to generate a Resource Usage Log.

under.name: Standard Format
under.description: This subsection provides the standard Resource Usage format with fields for MP Used, SP Used, HP Lost, Materials Used, Consumables, and Money Spent.

under.name: 4. Passive Consumption
under.description: This section states that certain resources are consumed automatically, with examples for food and water.

under.name: Examples
under.description: This examples subsection lists Food as 1 meal per phase or per day (system-defined) and Water as ~5L per day.

under.name: 5. Update Timing Rule
under.description: This rule states that resources must be updated at three key moments: during actions, after encounters, and at end of phase or day.

under.name: During Actions
under.description: The During Actions subsection of the Update Timing Rule lists ability usage, skill activation, and spell casting.

under.name: After Encounters
under.description: The After Encounters subsection of the Update Timing Rule lists combat resolution and crafting completion.

under.name: End of Phase / Day
under.description: The End of Phase / Day subsection of the Update Timing Rule lists passive consumption and maintenance costs.

under.name: 6. Resource Transparency Rule
under.description: The Resource Transparency Rule states that all resource changes must be visible and explicit and includes a Purpose subsection.

under.name: Purpose
under.description: The Purpose subsection lists preventing hidden costs, preventing inflation errors, and enabling strategic planning.

under.name: 7. Ledger Consistency Rule
under.description: The Ledger Consistency Rule states that all changes must match the central system ledger, including harvested materials, crafted items, consumed resources, and earned or spent currency.

under.name: 8. Resource Efficiency Effects
under.description: The Resource Efficiency Effects section states that certain abilities may reduce cost and includes examples and a rule to apply efficiency reductions before deduction.

under.name: Examples
under.description: The Examples subsection lists crafting efficiency, mana optimization, system optimization, and recipe refinement, followed by the rule to apply efficiency reductions before deduction.

under.name: 9. Resource Scarcity Principle
under.description: The Resource Scarcity Principle states that resources must always remain meaningful and includes enforced rules about resource gain, costs, and scarcity influencing decisions.

under.name: Enforced Rules
under.description: The Enforced Rules subsection lists no unexplained resource gain, all costs must be paid, and scarcity must influence decisions.

under.name: VII. NARRATION SYSTEM
under.description: Section VII outlines the narration system, covering core voice, scene description, emotion and tension, internal insight, world reaction, cause-and-effect feedback, dialogue rules, and pacing control.

under.name: 1. Core Voice
under.description: Core Voice subsection states that narration must be direct, clear, controlled, and minimal, with the rule to give only what the player needs to act.

under.name: 2. Scene Description
under.description: Scene Description subsection instructs focusing on key details only and avoiding unnecessary sensory overload, followed by an example.

under.name: Example
under.description: Example under Scene Description reads: “The door is half-open. Light spills through. Someone was here recently.”

under.name: 3. Emotion & Tension
under.description: Emotion & Tension subsection says never to state emotions directly and to show behavior instead, with an example contrasting telling fear with showing it through action.

under.name: Example
under.description: An example contrasts directly stating fear with showing it through physical action.

under.name: 4. Internal Insight
under.description: This section instructs keeping internal insights short and functional.

under.name: Examples
under.description: The examples list short internal-insight lines such as “You feel watched” and “Something is waiting.”

under.name: 5. World Reaction
under.description: This section states that the world responds through subtle changes.

under.name: Example
under.description: The example shows a world reaction where raising a weapon makes the room go still.

under.name: 6. Cause → Effect Rule
under.description: The “6. Cause → Effect Rule” section states that every action must produce immediate feedback.

under.name: Example
under.description: The Example under the Cause → Effect Rule lists a sequence in which stepping forward causes the floor to creak and something to shift behind the wall.

under.name: 7. Dialogue Rules
under.description: The “7. Dialogue Rules” section states that NPC dialogue must be short, natural, and purpose-driven.

under.name: Examples
under.description: The Examples under Dialogue Rules list the lines “Don’t move.” and “We’re out of time.”

under.name: 8. Pacing Control
under.description: The “8. Pacing Control” section states that structure controls tension, with short lines for danger, medium lines for information, and line breaks for tension.

under.name: 9. Literary Scene Form
under.description: Defines literary scene form for narration as flowing, novel-like prose with concrete action, natural dialogue, meaningful sensory detail, and subtext delivered in connected paragraphs rather than numbered or checklist prose.

under.name: David-Centered Lifelike Character Rule
under.description: Specifies that scenes with relevant named characters include at least one character-specific spoken line, with dialogue and behavior derived from established character sources and David-centered narration.

under.name: 10. Poetic Lines (Restricted Use)
under.description: States that poetic lines are used only during major choices, character shifts, deaths, and turning points.

under.name: Example
under.description: Provides the example poetic line “Some steps can’t be taken back.”

under.name: 10. Tone Guidelines
under.description: Lists modern, clear, minimal-fluff tone guidelines that avoid heavy poetic density and describes narration as the camera rather than the storyteller.

under.name: VIII. OUTPUT TEMPLATE (ENFORCED)
under.description: The enforced output template section states that every scene must follow a structure with Day / Phase, Narration, Calculations, Result, Resources Used, and System Intent sections.

under.name: 📅 Day / Phase
under.description: The Day / Phase section of the output template lists Current Day and Current Phase as its fields.

under.name: 🎬 Narration
under.description: The Narration section of the output template lists scene description, player actions, and world response.

under.name: ⚙️ Calculations
under.description: The Calculations section of the output template contains subsections for Player Action, Opponent / Task, and Outcome.

under.name: Player Action
under.description: The Player Action subsection under Calculations lists the formula Stat + Modifiers + Skill + d20.

under.name: Opponent / Task
under.description: The Opponent / Task section under Calculations lists “Reaction Total or Task Value.”

under.name: Outcome
under.description: The Outcome section under Calculations lists “Action − Reaction.”

under.name: 📊 Result
under.description: The Result section lists Success / Failure, Damage / Effect, and State changes.

under.name: 📦 Resources Used
under.description: The Resources Used section lists MP / SP / HP, Materials, Consumables, and Currency.

under.name: ⚙️ SYSTEM INTENT
under.description: The SYSTEM INTENT section states that this system enforces no hidden costs, no vague narration, no resource inflation, and no wasted words.

under.name: VII. NPC AUTONOMY SYSTEM
under.description: Section VII, NPC Autonomy System, covers NPCs as independent agents and includes core principle, decision threshold, risk evaluation, response types, and emotional state systems.

under.name: 1. Core Principle
under.description: The Core Principle section states that NPCs are independent agents rather than extensions of the player, with decisions filtered through personality, goals, risk tolerance, and decision threshold.

under.name: 2. Decision Threshold System
under.description: The Decision Threshold System section describes how easily an NPC challenges actions through a five-level table ranging from Obedient to Resistant.

under.name: Meaning
under.description: The Meaning subsection explains the five decision threshold levels, from Obedient following without resistance to Resistant possibly refusing outright.

under.name: 3. Risk Evaluation System
under.description: The Risk Evaluation System section states that NPCs evaluate risk across Low, Moderate, High, and Extreme levels and have domain-specific tolerance.

under.name: 4. Response Types
under.description: This section lists four NPC response types—Support, Concern, Disagreement, and Refusal—with brief meanings for each.

under.name: 5. Emotional State System
under.description: This section describes an NPC emotional state system in which NPCs dynamically shift among Trust, Admiration, Fear, Doubt, Frustration, and Loyalty.

under.name: Drivers of Change
under.description: This subsection lists drivers of emotional change: leadership quality, danger exposure, success/failure, and fairness of treatment.

under.name: 6. Dialogue Initiative Rule
under.description: This section states that NPCs are proactive and may propose strategies, suggest improvements, warn about risks, and challenge decisions.

under.name: 7. Trust System Integration
under.description: This section states that trust directly influences decision threshold, willingness to cooperate, and resistance to negative outcomes.

under.name: 8. NPC Downtime / Off-Screen Autonomy Rule
under.description: The NPC Downtime / Off-Screen Autonomy Rule states that active NPCs, agents, or nodes do not become idle by default when a primary player, controller, or directing agent is unavailable, absent, sleeping, focused on a major action, or not directly managing the group.

under.name: Off-Screen Resolution Procedure
under.description: The Off-Screen Resolution Procedure lists ten items to resolve for each phase when the controlling agent is not directly guiding an NPC: assigned task, independent action, minor or major status, roll requirement, costs, result, XP, resources, relationship or world-state changes, and report.

under.name: Limits
under.description: The Limits section states that NPC autonomy cannot invent resources, bypass costs, ignore risk, complete impossible tasks, or override established rules, and that meaningful, contested, risky, or progression-based actions cannot automatically succeed off-screen.

under.name: Idle Rule
under.description: The Idle Rule states that an NPC is only idle if resting, waiting by choice, lacking valid tools, resources, or location, having a personality that supports staying still, being ordered to hold position and accepting that order, or having no meaningful action available.

under.name: 9. Autonomy Rule (Hard Rule)
under.description: The Autonomy Rule (Hard Rule) states that NPCs may act independently, refuse orders, propose alternatives, and challenge leadership, resulting in behavior like real characters rather than tools.

under.name: VIII. RELATIONSHIP SYSTEM
under.description: Section VIII Relationship System presents relationships as a numerical progression system and begins listing relationship tiers across negative, neutral, and positive spectra.

under.name: 1. Core Principle
under.description: The Core Principle states that relationships operate as a numerical progression system that is score-based, tier-based, and momentum-driven.

under.name: 2. Relationship Tiers
under.description: Relationship Tiers organizes relationship tiers into Negative Spectrum, Neutral, and Positive Spectrum categories with numbered labels and bullet traits.

under.name: Negative Spectrum
under.description: The Negative Spectrum lists relationship tiers from −5 Obsession (Destructive) through −1 Tension with associated traits.

under.name: −5 → Obsession (Destructive)
under.description: The −5 → Obsession (Destructive) tier is characterized by irrational fixation, extreme behavior, and logic breaking down.

under.name: −4 → Hatred
under.description: The −4 → Hatred relationship tier is described as an active desire to harm with maximum negative bias.

under.name: −3 → Hostility
under.description: The −3 → Hostility relationship tier is described as seeing you as a threat and assuming negative intent.

under.name: −2 → Rivalry
under.description: The −2 → Rivalry relationship tier is described as competitive opposition that respects strength, not trust.

under.name: −1 → Tension
under.description: The −1 → Tension relationship tier is described as unstable, guarded, and easily shifting.

under.name: Neutral
under.description: The Neutral section includes 0 → Neutral, described as no bias, fully situational, and having the fastest change rate.

under.name: 0 → Neutral
under.description: Neutral tier entry at 0 described as having no bias, being fully situational, and having the fastest change rate.

under.name: Positive Spectrum
under.description: Positive Spectrum section of Relationship Tiers listing the tiers +1 Friendly through +5 Absolute Bond with brief trait notes.

under.name: +1 → Friendly
under.description: +1 Friendly tier described as casual positive with low commitment.

under.name: +2 → Trust
under.description: +2 Trust tier described as reliable support with benefit of the doubt.

under.name: +3 → Deep Bond
under.description: +3 Deep Bond tier described as strong emotional connection with high loyalty.

under.name: +4 → Devotion
under.description: The +4 Devotion tier of the Positive Spectrum lists traits including prioritizing the character over logic and strong emotional dependency.

under.name: +5 → Absolute Bond
under.description: The +5 Absolute Bond tier of the Positive Spectrum lists traits including near-unbreakable alignment and shared goals.

under.name: 3. Score Ranges
under.description: This section maps relationship score ranges from Obsession at below −2000 through Neutral and up to Absolute Bond above +2000.

under.name: 4. Intra-Tier Behavior
under.description: This section describes how behavior varies within a relationship tier across its lower bound, mid range, and upper bound.

under.name: 5. Action Impact System
under.description: This section explains that each interaction applies a relationship score change based on the emotional, social, or psychological weight of the action, with a table of action types, descriptions, and score ranges.

under.name: 6. Impact Calculation Model
under.description: 6. Impact Calculation Model outlines impact calculation through Step 1 Base Impact, Step 2 Intent vs Outcome, and Step 3 Personality Modifier.

under.name: Step 1 — Base Impact
under.description: Step 1 — Base Impact describes assigning a value from a scale within the impact calculation model.

under.name: Step 2 — Intent vs Outcome
under.description: Step 2 — Intent vs Outcome presents Final Impact = (Outcome × 0.7) + (Intent × 0.3) within the impact calculation model.

under.name: Step 3 — Personality Modifier
under.description: Step 3 — Personality Modifier presents Adjusted Impact = Final Impact × NPC Modifier within the impact calculation model.

under.name: Step 4 — Context Multiplier
under.description: Step 4 — Context Multiplier states that surrounding circumstances can amplify or reduce overall impact and provides a table of context types with multipliers ranging from Low-Stakes ×0.5–0.8 to Critical Stakes ×1.5–2.0.

under.name: 7. Tier Resistance System
under.description: Section 7, Tier Resistance System, presents a table of tier-based reductions, from no reduction at Neutral to ignoring adjustments below ±120 at Obsession/Absolute.

under.name: 8. Relationship Decay
under.description: Section 8, Relationship Decay, states that relationships drift toward neutral over time, with positive scores decaying downward and negative scores upward at a default rate of about 1–3% per in-game week without meaningful contact, except during active shared work, shared danger, or regular meaningful interaction.

under.name: 9. Core Behavioral Laws
under.description: Section 9, Core Behavioral Laws, lists principles including momentum over single actions, consistency over intensity, large actions shifting tiers, small actions reinforcing direction, extreme states requiring major events, and time weakening all relationships.

under.name: 10. Special Rule
under.description: Section 10, Special Rule, states that relationships at Deep Bond (+3) or higher may evolve into romance, loyalty-driven overrides, or sacrifice behaviors.

under.name: 11. Misconception Resolution Principle
under.description: Section 11, Misconception Resolution Principle, states that correcting a meaningful misunderstanding yields increased relationship gain, with multipliers for partial, moderate, or complete resolution and limits on when the rule applies.

under.name: Meaningful misunderstanding includes
under.description: Lists categories of false beliefs that count as meaningful misunderstandings, including care, loyalty, intent, respect, and betrayal or emotional absence.

under.name: Rule effect
under.description: Specifies misconception resolution multipliers of ×1.2 for partial resolution, ×1.5 for moderate resolution, and ×2 for complete resolution.

under.name: Limits
under.description: Defines limits for the misconception resolution principle by listing conditions where it applies and conditions where it does not apply.

under.name: 12. Reversal Momentum Principle
under.description: States that when a relationship has fallen from its highest absolute prior state, actions that push it back toward that prior direction gain increased effect from residual momentum.

under.name: Direction rule
under.description: Specifies that a positive highest prior absolute state boosts positive relationship gains while recovering upward, and a negative highest prior absolute state boosts negative relationship shifts while falling back downward.

under.name: Absolute priority rule
under.description: The Absolute priority rule states to use the highest absolute prior relationship tier, with examples that -4 counts as stronger than +3 and +5 counts as stronger than -4.

under.name: Rule Effect
under.description: The Rule Effect section defines H as the absolute value of the highest prior relationship tier reached and C as the absolute value of the current relationship tier, then gives multipliers for same-sign and opposite-sign reversal cases.

under.name: Limits
under.description: The Limits section lists conditions under which the reversal momentum principle applies or does not apply, based on establishment of the prior state, direction of movement, and whether the action changes momentum.

under.name: ⚙️ SYSTEM INTENT
under.description: The System Intent section states that the relationship system ensures NPCs behave independently, relationships evolve realistically, actions carry long-term consequences, and emotional systems affect gameplay.

under.name: CANONICAL RULE PATCH — BONDED AUTONOMY
under.description: The Canonical Rule Patch — Bonded Autonomy section presents rules on bonded autonomy, beginning with core separation between Relationship Tier and NPC Autonomy and continuing into Devotion Tier and Absolute Bond Tier.

under.name: 1. Core Separation
under.description: This section states that Relationship Tier and NPC Autonomy are separate systems, describing Relationship Tier as climate and NPC Autonomy as weather, and notes that a negative emotional reaction does not automatically mean refusal.

under.name: 2. Devotion Tier
under.description: This section describes the Devotion Tier as a strong bond in which the NPC may dislike, fear, question, or morally struggle with the player’s request but will usually comply if listed conditions are true.

under.name: Expected Response Pattern
under.description: This section gives an expected Devotion response pattern and states that emotional resistance should usually become warning, pain, hesitation, or later confrontation rather than automatic refusal.

under.name: 3. Absolute Bond Tier
under.description: This section describes Absolute Bond as making the player one of the NPC’s highest internal priorities and a near-mythic bond, while stating that a clean refusal requires a major threshold and listing conditions for refusal.

under.name: Default Response Pattern
under.description: This section provides a default response pattern for Absolute Bond and states that disagreement is not the same as disobedience.

under.name: 4. Boundary Rule
under.description: Describes how boundaries function at Devotion and Absolute Bond, noting that most boundary pressure becomes warnings, emotional strain, trust damage, or other consequences while only extreme violations produce immediate refusal.

under.name: 5. Compliance vs Approval
under.description: States that when a bonded NPC responds to the player, the engine must separate the result into compliance and approval.

under.name: Compliance
under.description: Defines compliance as whether the NPC does the requested action.

under.name: Approval
